I don’t understand why the consensus is against a 24 team playoff, I personally think it’s awesome. The issue has never been the amount of teams, but the arbitrary capricious methodology implemented in selecting who is awarded the opportunity to compete for a championship. If they had more automatic qualifiers, I think this 24 playoff system would be perfect and I think it’s the right number of total teams.

There is this wrong notion that it’s going to automatically and implicitly trivialize the value of the regular season. The value of the regular season is much more contingent on the methodology of how teams are selected then the total number of teams as a whole.

There is also a big fat financial incentive that Josh‘s misappropriating whenever ascertaining what the fans actually want. I bet you don’t stop watching the games because of it and that’s what their bottom line number is not forums on your podcast and qualitative based focus groups.

Bottom line, I just strongly disagree that expanding the playoff inherently and categorically diminishes the value of the regular season. That doesn’t make any sense when we’re not putting it up against some sort of objective criteria. The methodology of selecting teams is inherently more significant than the records of the teams themselves, and I don’t know why people don’t understand this.

The SEC and Big Ten each organized into FOUR divisions, with every division champion guaranteed a playoff spot? The Big 12 and ACC each organize into TWO divisions, also with guaranteed spots. Keep the G6 guarantee, add 11 at-large bids, and you've got a 24-team playoff!

Here's the BONUS: You encourage regional scheduling AND bring back meaningful championships within these mega-conferences!

Remember when the SWC, Big 8, and SEC crowned champions WITHOUT championship games? It worked because the conferences were smaller, just as these new divisions would be.

And I CHECKED THE NUMBERS! From 2015 through 2025, NOT ONE division champion under my proposed alignments would have finished outside the Top 25.

We could expand the playoff, restore regional rivalries, and make winning your division MEAN SOMETHING again!

Love the show. But this expansion isn’t what kills CFB. The death blow had already been made in NIL and the Transfer Portal. Your forehead vein is popping out wanting to save something that is already dead. This expansion is what the powers that be hope to use to keep the flies off the corpse a little while longer by generating talk of seeding, home playoff games, and bye weeks. When that novelty wears off, game over. 

Not one single CFB fan I know feels the same about the game, and that has nothing  to do with this expansion. So while your arguments are cogent and well articulated, Pandora’s box was already opened and the obituary has already been written.  People will watch their favorite teams but the days of watching CFB all day Saturday, just for the love of the game, have passed for  the regular fan. 

Just my opinion.

text: So, Josh. How is the National Champion determined in College Basketball? Yeah, that's right: Through a now-76-team playoff, wherein ALL 32 conference champions get automatic bids. (There are 363 D-1 Schools, as opposed to 138 FBS schools.) And yes, the champion is determined through a "one-and-done" elimination process -- not unlike earlier football-playoff iterations. My point is simply that the greatly-expanded NCAA Basketball Tournament ("March Madness") is HUGELY popular across the company, with people at offices across the fruited plain filling out brackets - people who know nothing about the teams, the sport, etc., but STILL watch the tournament. So having 24 teams (we should have 40, just like D-3 Football does) will in no way harm the regular season. We should KEEP Conference Championships, and CONTINUE to make them the automatic qualifiers.

Unlike most other things in life, there's an objective measure of success in football, and it's clear that in the age of dispersed talent under NIL, money alone can never be the way to that success.

text_body:
For those who make the 24-team playoff, there is a greater perfection to pursue, namely the next game; the championship, if they go so far. Every team that makes it will try as hard as they can to prove themselves. For those remaining bowl-eligible teams that fail to make it, there will be bowl games to play, just as before.
Besides, it's a better sport when the average team has taken greater losses - the parity makes for more exciting games, and NIL makes parity inevitable. An expanded playoff deals handily with the consequences of this. It also devalues the P4 conference championships, which may help to bring about a pragmatic, geographic realignment of the conferences.
There's lots to like here.

I'm 72. And, honestly, I miss College Football as it used to be 30+ years ago. 

Even then there were issues. I doubt that the sport has ever been pristine. 

But, somewhere along the way the emphasis changed from pursuing an education and becoming good, productive citizens to "make as much money as you can."  

And now, with the portal and NIL, it's feeling more like a AAA league, a farm team for the NFL.

Yet, college ball is still a lot better than the NFL. And, as long as colleges can continue to maintain their various traditions in connection with the sport it will always be better. 

But, I do miss the "good ol' days."

Of course we can. The goal, as it should be every year, is to win your conference. It doesn't matter how mnay teams a conference has because the cream will rise to the top. Also, every team doesn't have to play each other through a season. While we can take some cues from the NFL, we can't duplicate this in a realistic way. 

What we can do however, is deal with what we got and understand that the playoff isn't the goal. The goal is to win your conference. The goal is to make the regular season mean something again. The players will need contracts that can't be stymied by a local judge or some money grubbing lawyer just like the NFL has. CFB needs rules that can't be questioned or litigated. 

CFB is a professional league now, filled with professional players with no rules except you need to go to that school. Yet here we are trying to make sense of a system that no longer exists. This new professional league needs to crown a champion based on what happens on the field not a beauty contest where people who don't even play the game decide who gets in and who gets left out. This needs to stop. I'm just offering one way to do this while keeping the real gen of CFB ... the regular season ... intact.

@BlakeRamone-c1t Since Lester took over in the 2024-2025 season, Iowa has been averaging about 30 pts a game. After losing about 18 player in the offseason - #1 OL and a top tier DL - they’re a young, inexperienced team, but development has been notable. It’ll likely be like last year where they go to a bowl game and beat another SEC team whining that they didn’t make the playoffs. I hope the OC’s first QB recruit is ready to go next year. Sucks relying on an NIL QB when you don’t have the funds of those blue blood teams. 

TBH, I’m pretty tired of this claim of SEC being so deep because they’re beating the crap out of each other, while B1G is so bad for the same reason. It’s all assumptions based on a few early season games and influenced media opinions. What media corporation has the most revenue, and who’s most beneficial for them to encourage in the rankings? ESPN by far, and to think they don’t use influence to make more is like thinking large corporations don’t use influence on political decisions to profit themselves. I’ll believe the hype when it’s proven in the playoffs and bowl games, but it’s only been hype the past few years. Really seems the mid teams are just getting more competitive by knowing how to use NIL best with their programs. There’s some really good younger coaches out there too that those blue bloods will likely be trying to buy after a few seasons of playoff flops. A 9-3 team in one conference would still likely be 9-3 in another. TX would still have flopped to 2 much lesser teams in B1G, and Indiana would still have found ways to squeak out wins in the SEC. How many 60+ yd FG’s have been made in the SEC this season?

text: The narrative that Miami "figured out" Notre Dame’s defense is a total myth that completely ignores what actually happened on the field. When the Irish were pressing and throwing the ball, they dominated their way to a 24–3 lead, but they intentionally shifted to hyper-conservative play-calling and clock management rather than continuing to hunt for touchdowns. In fact, Notre Dame ran the ball twice as much in the second half as they did in the first, completely bleeding the clock dry by chewing up over 9 minutes of game time on rushing sequences compared to just 4 minutes on pass plays. On top of that, Miami's sudden offensive spark only happened because All-American cornerback Leonard Moore was forced to the medical tent with an eye poke; the Hurricanes scored their first two touchdowns directly against a backup, but the moment Moore returned to the field, the Irish locked it down and forced the game-winning 4th-down stop. Miami didn't mount a tactical comeback—they got incredibly lucky that Notre Dame took its foot off the gas to shorten the game, because if the Irish kept pressing with a healthy starting lineup, this game easily ends up a 38–17 blowout.

The SEC dominates the top 25 because its schools have played the toughest schedules. The schedules are the toughest because the SEC's schools dominate the top 25. Chicken, egg.

The true genius of schedule strength is that it's a machine fueled by hyperbole and repetition, and it exists in a locker room where teams can neither enter nor exit. It is a room populated with the name brands, the ones we all accepted a decade ago were good because they had the pedigree, and no matter how much Wake Forest, Texas Tech or Boise State bang on the door, they'll never be let in.

Never mind that the ACC was 8-6 vs. the SEC last year. Never mind that the SEC hasn't had a team play for a national championship in the past three years. Never mind that Texas A&M and Oklahoma were top-10 teams to open the season but turned out to be pretty bad. (The same can be said for the Big10, where Penn State, Michigan, and Washington still manage to prop up teams' schedules long after being exposed as frauds.)

ACC has a bunch of 6-3 or better teams and only two ranked. The entire process is a charade. 24-teams just means more SEC (and maybe Big10) teams get into the invitational.

text: At the end of the day, the playoff should be about identifying the best teams in the country and determining who has the ability to compete for and win a national championship. Strength of schedule absolutely matters, but it shouldn't be the only determining factor. We also have to consider overall performance, talent, coaching, quality wins, and the eye test. A team shouldn't automatically be penalized for a weaker schedule if it has consistently demonstrated that it can compete with the best. Likewise, a team shouldn't automatically be rewarded for playing a difficult schedule if it hasn't performed at the level expected. The real question should be: If these teams lined up against each other on a neutral field, who has the best chance of winning? Rankings should reflect the complete body of work while also recognizing which teams are genuinely capable of making a championship run. Ultimately, we're selecting playoff teams, not handing out awards for the toughest schedule.

text_body:
Yes, a rigged system produces rigged results. When draft classes and transfer portals are rigged to give extra stars to the SEC (and about eight other teams), of course more of them will start ranked, boosting the reputation of wins… and we know the cycle. 

Go watch the transfer portal. When a player moves to an SEC school, they almost always get a star added. It doesn’t get added at the end of the season, at the time they enter the portal, or at the time they are in the portal. It gets added when they see where the player signed. And it works the other way too. If a player moves from the SEC or the Big Ten to the ACC or the Big 12, they almost always get docked a star simply because of where they signed. 

Rigged system produces rigged results.
